Join us this Saturday morning at Greenway Farm from 7 - 11 am for an educational workshop all about bird banding!  What is bird banding, you ask? In order to identify and keep track of individual birds, scientists put aluminum or colored bands on birds' legs. Similar to the license plate on a car, each aluminum band is engraved with a unique set of numbers. This helps us track important data such as migratory paths, general health, and lifespan. This is a FREE all-ages workshop. Please share with your bird-loving friends and family. We would love an incredible turn out for this fun event.

CPD Investigating Deadly Crash Involving Pedestrians on E Main St. CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is investigating a deadly crash involving pedestrians that resulted in one woman's death. At approximately 9:20 p.m. Saturday, CPD's Traffic Unit responded to reports of a crash involving pedestrians in the 300 block of E Main Street. The preliminary investigation indicates a group of people were using a crosswalk when a pickup truck hit two individuals.  Hamilton County EMS transported both patients to the hospital. One victim was treated for non-life threatening injuries. The other victim, an 88-year-old woman, later succumbed to her injuries.  The driver, Reginald Cousins Jr (DOB: 11/16/1966), was arrested and charged with Driving Under the Influence, Aggravated Assault, Reckless Endangerment, Vehicular Assault, Pedestrians' Right-of-Way in Crosswalks, Failure to Exercise Due Care, and Light Law Violation. Additional charges are pending.  This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. Chattanooga Police ask anyone with information regarding this incident to call 423-698-2525. The charges and allegations referenced in this release are merely accusations of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted through due process of law. #CPDnews

Salary: $23.19 - $28.02 per hour (GS.8) Work Hours: Monday - Friday, 8:00 A.M. - 4:30 P.M. (EST) *Hours may vary due to work assignments and projects.* Work Location: 4063 N Hawthorne Street, Chattanooga, TN FLSA Status: This is a Non-Exempt position. Department: Public Works- Solid Waste CLASSIFICATION SUMMARY: Incumbents in this classification drive and operate commercial vehicles, tractors, and other equipment with specialized functions that involve the operation of mechanisms to complete tasks in addition to driving and maneuvering the vehicle in order to complete tasks for various solid waste collection, maintenance, forestry and construction projects. Equipment in this classification includes commercial larger vehicles requiring a higher level of skill to drive and maneuver through small residential roads and vehicles with mechanisms that are somewhat complex to operate, requiring more dexterity and finesse. Classification is reserved for those positions where the driving and operating of included equipment is the primary function of the job. SERIES LEVEL: Truck Driver is a stand-alone position. ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS: ( The following duties ARE NOT intended to serve as a comprehensive list of all duties performed by all employees in this classification, only a representative summary of the primary duties and responsibilities. Incumbent(s) may not be required to perform all duties listed and may be required to perform additional, position-specific duties.) Operates various equipment and vehicles to complete tasks related to the maintenance, upkeep, installation and construction of city grounds, property, utilities, rights-of-way, and other infrastructure for Public Works; drives vehicles over public roads, worksites, right-of-way, parks, public works facilities, and other city property; maneuvers in and around traffic, parked cars, equipment, utilities, and other obstacles; obeys all traffic laws and safety guidelines, monitors immediate environment and work are to ensure the safety of the operator, other workers, the equipment and the public. Some positions may drive tandem and tri-axle dump trucks to transport and haul materials between original and final destinations for use in maintenance and construction projects; positions vehicle to allow for the most efficient and effective loading or dumping of materials; secures all doors, gates, and fasteners to prevent spillage or loss of load; operates dumping mechanism to dump materials at appropriate locations. Operates mowing tractors with articulated boom mowing system to mow rights-of-way and other City property along steep slopes, ditches, and hard-to-reach areas inaccessible to most mowing apparatuses; scouts path for and removes rocks, debris and other obstacles that may cause damage to the equipment, property or the public; determines proper settings and adjusts boom for the proper angle, height, and trajectory; maneuvers and monitors boom mower for optimal operation. Operate knuckle-boom truck to collect trash, limbs and other debris from work sites, parks, and other City property and transport it to the landfill; positions vehicle alongside targeted debris; operates truck- or trailer-mounted knuckle-boom arm to pick up debris and load it into the truck; secures all doors, gates, and fasteners to prevent spillage or loss of load during transport; dumps material at an appropriate location. Operates and maneuvers knuckle-boom and articulated arm to pick up limbs; maintains a constant awareness of the environment to ensure the safety of the operator, other crew workers, and the public. Operates street sweepers along a prescribed route to remove dirt and debris from City streets and parking lots; maneuvers in and out of traffic and around parked cars, taking care to reduce congestion and maintain safety; determines proper settings and adjusts brushes for proper angle and height, maintaining proper curb distance for optimum coverage. Drives low-boy and other tractor-trailer rigs to transport heavy construction equipment and materials to and from work-sites; maneuvers equipment to load and unload from the trailer, operating mechanisms as necessary to position for safe transportation. Drives a variety of garbage trucks along a prescribed commercial or residential route to collect refuse; makes frequent stops at appropriate intervals to position truck near refuse containers; retrieves refuse container and attaches to automated dumping mechanism; dumps refuse and returns container; maintains the pace of collection activities to ensure timely completion of the assigned route. Drives fuel truck to transport fuel to equipment at work sites; operates the mechanism to fuel equipment as necessary; applies knowledge of hazardous materials when transporting, handling, and responding to spills involving gasoline, diesel fuel, and other flammable/volatile liquids. Drives bucket and/or lift truck to work site and operates lift mechanisms to elevate crews performing various maintenance, upkeep and installation for traffic systems, tree trimming and other tasks requiring access to high places; positions vehicle and lift-platform to ensure optimum access to the required location and avoid power lines, low branches, traffic and other hazards; monitors activities to ensure the safety of crew workers. Operates a jet-flushing/vacuum/viewer truck for the purpose of cleaning out storm drain and sanitary sewer pipe, manholes, catch basins and other brick and concrete drainage structures in order to maintain the flow throughout the stormwater drainage and sewer waste systems. Drives trucks with a side-mounted articulated vacuum boom along an assigned route for the purpose of picking up leaves, litter, and other yard waste from rights-of-way and out of drainage measurements in order to maintain stormwater drainage flow throughout the entire system. Inspects and prepares equipment for safe and proper operation prior to beginning work for the day; performs light maintenance on equipment which includes refueling and refilling lubricants; cleans vehicles, beds, and mounted equipment upon completion of assignments; secures vehicle after use. Sanitize and clean assigned equipment daily. Performs basic and semi-skilled labor as appropriate to assist in the completion of maintenance, upkeep and construction projects; picks up paper, limbs and other debris; uses hand tools and operates motorized tools as necessary to complete the assigned task. May remove dead animals and trees from the right of way as well as public roads. May answer 911 emergency calls for oil spills as well as black ice. May assist in contacting departments or personnel for an emergency situation. May be required to use, carry and answer cell phones, other devices, and/or two-way radio as determined by their job duties and their supervisor. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. May be assigned or reassigned to any division within the department. Performs other related duties as required. This position is deemed essential during inclement weather situations, and must report to or remain at work, even when administrative closings are announced, as determined by the Department Head. DEPARTMENT SPECIFIC DUTIES (if any): When working in Forestry division: Uses of chainsaws, rigging lines, pulleys, and cranes. Working in high traffic areas with the use of signs, cones, and flaggers and in the vicinity of power lines, moving traffic or directly above buildings. Removes and cleans up dead or hazardous trees. Available on call for storm work or downed trees. May train personnel. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: High School Diploma or GED and one (1) year of any combination of relevant education, experience, and/or training sufficient to successfully perform the essential functions of this job; or any combination of equivalent experience and education. LICENSING AND CERTIFICATIONS: Valid Class A, Class A restricted or Class B commercial driver license. Requires appropriate license endorsement(s) related to the area of assignment. KNOWLEDGE SKILLS: Knowledge of occupational hazards and safety precautions; general equipment and maintenance principles; materials and equipment utilized in assigned area of responsibility; demonstrated ability to drive and operate assigned equipment; operation of commercial vehicles that consist of self-contained specialized equipment. Typical equipment operated might include, but is not limited to: tractor-trailers, low boys, fuel trucks, bucket trucks, mechanical street sweepers, knuckle-boom trucks, articulated boom mowers, oil distributors, jet-flushing/vacuum trucks, CCTV equipped trucks and automated garbage trucks with an articulated arm. Must be able to use electronic devices to receive and track work. Position requires minimal, but daily public interaction and must be customer service centered, focused, and able to recognize or resolve customer needs according to departmental practices. PHYSICAL DEMANDS: Positions in this class typically require climbing, balancing, stooping, kneeling, crouching, crawling, reaching, standing, walking, pushing, pulling, lifting, fingering, grasping, feeling, talking, hearing, seeing and repetitive motions. WORK ENVIRONMENT: Medium Work: Exerting up-to 50 pounds of force occasionally, and/or up-to 20 pounds of force frequently, and/or up-to 10 pounds of force constantly to move objects. In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, the City will provide reasonable accommodations to qualified individuals with disabilities and encourage both prospective and current employees to discuss potential accommodations with the employer. Drives bucket and/or lift truck to work site and operates lift mechanisms to elevate crews performing various maintenance, upkeep and installation for traffic systems, tree trimming and other tasks requiring access to high places; positions vehicle and lift-platform to ensure optimum access to the required location and avoid power lines, low branches, traffic and other hazards; monitors activities to ensure the safety of crew workers. Operates a jet-flushing/vacuum/viewer truck for the purpose of cleaning out storm drain and sanitary sewer pipe, manholes, catch basins and other brick and concrete drainage structures in order to maintain the flow throughout the stormwater drainage and sewer waste systems. Drives trucks with a side-mounted articulated vacuum boom along an assigned route for the purpose of picking up leaves, litter, and other yard waste from rights-of-way and out of drainage measurements in order to maintain stormwater drainage flow throughout the entire system. Inspects and prepares equipment for safe and proper operation prior to beginning work for the day; performs light maintenance on equipment which includes refueling and refilling lubricants; cleans vehicles, beds, and mounted equipment upon completion of assignments; secures vehicle after use. Sanitize and clean assigned equipment daily. Performs basic and semi-skilled labor as appropriate to assist in the completion of maintenance, upkeep and construction projects; picks up paper, limbs and other debris; uses hand tools and operates motorized tools as necessary to complete the assigned task. May remove dead animals and trees from the right of way as well as public roads. May answer 911 emergency calls for oil spills as well as black ice. May assist in contacting departments or personnel for an emergency situation. May be required to use, carry and answer cell phones, other devices, and/or two-way radio as determined by their job duties and their supervisor. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. May be assigned or reassigned to any division within the department. Performs other related duties as required. This position is deemed essential during inclement weather situations, and must report to or remain at work, even when administrative closings are announced, as determined by the Department Head. DEPARTMENT SPECIFIC DUTIES (if any): When working in Forestry division: Uses of chainsaws, rigging lines, pulleys, and cranes. Working in high traffic areas with the use of signs, cones, and flaggers and in the vicinity of power lines, moving traffic or directly above buildings. Removes and cleans up dead or hazardous trees. Available on call for storm work or downed trees. May train personnel. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: High School Diploma or GED and one (1) year of any combination of relevant education, experience, and/or training sufficient to successfully perform the essential functions of this job; or any combination of equivalent experience and education. LICENSING AND CERTIFICATIONS: Valid Class A, Class A restricted or Class B commercial driver license. Requires appropriate license endorsement(s) related to the area of assignment. KNOWLEDGE SKILLS: Knowledge of occupational hazards and safety precautions; general equipment and maintenance principles; materials and equipment utilized in assigned area of responsibility; demonstrated ability to drive and operate assigned equipment; operation of commercial vehicles that consist of self-contained specialized equipment. Typical equipment operated might include, but is not limited to: tractor-trailers, low boys, fuel trucks, bucket trucks, mechanical street sweepers, knuckle-boom trucks, articulated boom mowers, oil distributors, jet-flushing/vacuum trucks, CCTV equipped trucks and automated garbage trucks with an articulated arm. Must be able to use electronic devices to receive and track work. Position requires minimal, but daily public interaction and must be customer service centered, focused, and able to recognize or resolve customer needs according to departmental practices. PHYSICAL DEMANDS: Positions in this class typically require climbing, balancing, stooping, kneeling, crouching, crawling, reaching, standing, walking, pushing, pulling, lifting, fingering, grasping, feeling, talking, hearing, seeing and repetitive motions. WORK ENVIRONMENT: Medium Work: Exerting up-to 50 pounds of force occasionally, and/or up-to 20 pounds of force frequently, and/or up-to 10 pounds of force constantly to move objects. It was a busy morning for the Chattanooga Fire Department as firefighters fought back-to-back house fires.  The first fire was reported at 8:47 AM on 10/13/26 at a duplex in the 1800 block of Citico Avenue in the East Chattanooga area. First arriving units found smoke and fire coming from the back of the structure. Firefighters initiated an interior attack and took another line to the rear of the residence where flames were through the collapsed roof. Searches were conducted and no one was found inside on either side of the duplex. Fire officials learned that both sides were vacant. By 9:10 AM, the fire was out.  Engine 4, Engine 5, Engine 10, Squad 1, Ladder 1, Battalion 1, Battalion 3, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EPB. There were no injuries.  As crews were wrapping up operations on Citico Avenue, another house fire was reported at 9:29 AM in the 1500 block of South Highland Park Avenue off Main Street. Callers to 911 indicated that flames were visible through the front doors and windows of the home. A plume of smoke could be seen by responding companies. On the scene, crews found fire in the front of the structure. Officials quickly learned that one person was home at the time of the fire, but they made it out safely. Primary attack was made through the front door and crews continued working to extinguish the blaze. Their efforts were made difficult by the amount of contents inside the residence. By 10:01 AM, the fire was out. One adult was displaced and will be receiving assistance from the American Red Cross. The cause of the fire is under investigation.  Engine 1, Squad 13, Engine 9, Engine 14, Squad 1, Engine 5, Squad 20, Engine 3, Battalion 1, Battalion 2, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EBP. There were no injuries.  Fire investigators do not believe the two fires are connected in any way. Thanks to Red Shift companies for their hard work and adaptability in moving from one response to another.

On Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we’re highlighting a powerful story found within one of Chattanooga’s most meaningful public artworks. At the bottom of The Passage at Ross’s Landing, a steel water spider rests beneath the shallow pool. Designed by Cherokee artist Demos Glass, the sculpture draws inspiration from ancient shell carvings discovered at the Dallas archaeological site right here in Hamilton County. In Cherokee storytelling, the Water Spider helped bring fire to the world when other animals could not. Using a small bowl she wove and carried on her back, she crossed the water, collected an ember, and returned with the gift of fire. Her story is one of courage, ingenuity, and perseverance. Created in 2005 by Team Gadugi, a group of Cherokee artists, The Passage honors Indigenous history, culture, and the Cherokee people whose forced removal is part of Chattanooga’s history. Today, we honor the Indigenous peoples who have called this region home for generations and the Native communities whose cultures, stories, and artistic traditions continue to thrive. The next time you visit The Passage, take a closer look. There are stories beneath the surface. #IndigenousPeoplesDay #PublicArtChattanooga #ThePassage #Chattanooga

HONORING OUR FALLEN: Senior Firefighter Chad Crisp was added to the Tennessee Fallen Firefighter Memorial in Bell Buckle, TN this past weekend. We lost Chad in 2020 after a brave battle with occupational cancer.  For the Crisp family, it was incredibly special to see Chad remembered in this way. His wife, Leah, wrote this: “While we honor Chad and his lifelong dedication to service, we also want to recognize the advocates who worked tirelessly to change policy so Chad could be included. Changes to presumptive illness laws at both the state and federal levels have started closing the gap in coverage for so many fire families facing a cancer diagnosis. Perhaps the most significant change is happening right here at home. The City of Chattanooga now includes comprehensive cancer coverage in its worker's compensation policy for firefighters—covering all types of cancer. To my knowledge, this level of coverage is limited to only a couple of municipalities statewide. Additionally, the Chattanooga Fire Department has implemented new safety procedures and early detection screenings to protect our firefighters. Chattanooga put words into action, providing meaningful support for firefighters and their families when it matters most. As we remember Chad, we also celebrate the dedication of those who continue to honor his memory by creating a safer path for those who follow in his footsteps.”

CHECK YOUR INBOX! 📩 TDHS has begun sending invitations to apply for child care assistance, and families have 14 days to respond! ⏰ If you or someone you know has been waiting for help with childcare costs, please check your email carefully, including your spam and junk folders. An important message like this can be easy to miss! ❤️ Please share this post! Someone in our community could miss an opportunity simply because they didn’t see the email in time. Childcare assistance can make a life-changing difference for families trying to work, go to school, and provide a better future for their children. Let’s make sure the word gets out!Progress for Tennessee families! Let’s keep it going. The Tennessee Department of Human Services has begun inviting families on the Smart Steps child care waitlist to apply for assistance. We welcome this step. For families who qualify, help paying for child care could mean being able to stay in a job, continue their education and give their children a strong start. 📣 On the Smart Steps waitlist?  Watch your email for an official invitation from TDHS Child Care Services. Families who receive an invitation have 14 days to respond and submit an application. Approval depends on eligibility. After the response window closes for the first 100 or so people contacted, TDHS will reach out to the next group of families. These invitations are encouraging, and the need remains substantial. According to the Tennessee Commission on Children and Youth, 9,546 families, representing 13,835 children, were on the waitlist as of June 2, 2026. Behind those numbers are parents trying to afford the child care they need to work or attend school, and children who could benefit from quality early learning. There is something powerful about local childcare providers coming together, sharing their experiences, and having honest conversations about the future of childcare in our community. Our providers are more than business owners. They are educators, advocates, and an essential part of the village raising our children. When they come together, we have an opportunity to listen, identify challenges, share solutions, and build a path forward that supports both families and the people who care for our youngest learners. The challenges facing childcare are real, but so is the power of collaboration, community, and collective action. We may not have every answer today, but by bringing the right people to the table, we can begin turning conversations into meaningful change. This is about more than childcare. It’s about our children, our families, our providers, and the future of our community. The future is worth fighting for, and together, we can build something better.  #ChildcareMatters #EarlyLearning

Today marked the final scenario day for the Chattanooga Fire Department's 80-hour Structural Collapse Specialist class! Since September 28, firefighters from both the Chattanooga and Cleveland Fire Departments have put in long hours every day—including through the weekend—to master heavy rescue and structural collapse operations. Throughout the course, members learned:   Lifting and Moving: Relocate massive debris using prybars, 4x4 cribbing, and rollers.  Breaking and Breaching: Penetrate reinforced concrete and heavy materials using specialized CFD rescue tools.  Shoring Systems: Construct complex lateral and horizontal shores to stabilize compromised buildings and secure safe entry routes. Today’s scenario was a well-earned "victory lap" to put all these skills together. Thank you to these dedicated students for their hard work and commitment. Through continuous training like this, our departments are better prepared to serve and protect Chattanooga, Cleveland, and our surrounding regional communities. Great job, everyone!

Friends, Many of you have reached out with questions about the plaques on the Walnut Street Bridge. Crews continue working daily to return each existing plaque to its original location following the renovation. It’s a long process with hundreds of plaques.  Prior to the renovation, several plaques were already missing. Efforts were made to locate those plaques and list of names through the original program, but unfortunately, they could not be recovered. To avoid leaving visible gaps, some of the remaining plaques were repositioned closer together. The organization that originally administered the plaque program, Friends of The Walnut Street Bridge, is no longer offering plaques. As contracts are finalized and the necessary paperwork is completed, no additional features or plaques will be added to the bridge. This could take a good year. At this time, it is uncertain whether the non profit partner will bring back plaque program.

Join the City of Chattanooga Team Chattanooga , a vibrant and growing community of over 190,000 residents within a metropolitan area of nearly 600,000 is known as the "Scenic City" for a reason. The Chattanooga Fire Department is teaming up with the National Fire Protection Association to support Fire Prevention Week 2026. This year’s FPW theme, “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” focuses on the simple steps people can take to recharge safely. Safe charging means making smart choices every time you plug in. Many devices used in our daily lives - phones, tablets, laptops, tools, toys, e-bikes, and scooters—run on rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which store a lot of energy in a small space. If they are damaged or charged the wrong way, they can overheat, start a fire, or even explode. • Use the cord and charger that came with your device or one approved by the manufacturer. Using the wrong charger can damage the battery and increase the risk of fire. • Charge devices on a table, desk, or other hard, flat surface. Do not charge them on beds, couches, or under pillows. Devices and chargers produce heat during normal charging. Soft surfaces can trap heat and block airflow, which can cause the battery to overheat. • Stop using your device if it feels very hot, starts to swell, is smoking, or has a strange smell. These are warning signs that the battery may be damaged or failing. • Unplug your device when it is fully charged. Do not leave it plugged in longer than needed. Leaving a device plugged in too long can increase heat and stress on the battery. • Charge larger items like e-bikes, scooters, and power tools outside and away from exits. These batteries are larger and store more energy. If they fail, fires can grow quickly and spread.  • When on a plane, keep your device where you can see it while charging. Do not charge devices in overhead compartments. Do not charge e-cigarettes or vapes on a plane. If a battery overheats or fails, it is important for the flight crew to respond quickly.

Today, we celebrated a century of tradition, recreation and community at Brainerd Golf Course, and we couldn’t have asked for a better group to celebrate with, even with a little rain! Opened on October 3, 1926, Brainerd was designed by legendary golf architect Donald Ross and created with a simple vision: to provide quality, accessible outdoor recreation for the Chattanooga community. One hundred years later, that mission continues. Generations of golfers have made memories on these fairways, and Brainerd remains an important part of Chattanooga’s public golf tradition. Special shout out to Greta Hayes-Director of Recreation, Eddie Taylor-Director of Golf, Joe Starr-Director of Maintenance and Edwin Prichard-Brainerd Golf Manager. Combined, these individuals have over 115 years of service with City of Chattanooga golf.  Also thank you Mayor Kelly and District 5 Councilman Dennis Clark for sharing a few words.  A huge thank you to everyone who came out today, played in the 100 Year Celebration Two-Person Scramble, cheered on the players and helped us celebrate this incredible milestone. Here’s to 100 years of Brainerd Golf, and many more to come!

Join the City of Chattanooga Team Chattanooga , a vibrant and growing community of over 190,000 residents within a metropolitan area of nearly 600,000 is known as the "Scenic City" for a reason. Nestled along the Tennessee River and surrounded by the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains, we are a hub of outdoor adventure and innovation. Home to the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga (UTC) and Chattanooga State Community College , our city blends a rich industrial history with a tech-forward future—famously powered by the nation’s first community-wide "Gig" fiber-optic network.​ The City of Chattanooga was also recently designated as a "National Park City,” the first of its kind in the United States. Our Organization As a City, we are powered by a dedicated workforce of approximately ​ 2,600 employees committed to excellence in public service and making Chattanooga the best community in the country. Our team ensures our city thrives through a wide range of municipal services, including: Public Safety: Chattanooga Police and Fire Departments. Infrastructure Utilities: Public Works, Waste Resources, and specialized Stormwater management. Quality of Life: Award-winning Parks and Outdoors and Community Development systems and the Chattanooga Public Library. Transportation: The Chattanooga Metropolitan Airport (CHA) and citywide transit and pedestrian friendly initiatives. Innovation: Leading-edge smart-city programs with a commitment to cutting edge workforce development policies to ensure all our residents can get ahead. Why Choose Chattanooga? The City of Chattanooga’s workforce is the heartbeat of our community. We don't just offer jobs; we offer careers with purpose: making Chattanooga the best city in America. We are committed to being the premier employer of choice in Southeast Tennessee by providing: Competitive Compensation: Robust pay scales that reflect our commitment to our staff. Work-Life Balance: Generous paid time off and flexible scheduling where possible. Exceptional Wellness: Comprehensive health benefits and wellness programs designed for you and your family that deliver savings to you beyond your paycheck, featuring a centralized health clinic and pharmacy for all City employees. . Growth: A focus on professional development and upward mobility within the organization. ​The Great Outdoors: Your Backyard Playground: Chattanooga isn't just near nature, it's immersed in it. As one of the most biodiverse cities in North America, the "Scenic City" offers an ecological richness that few places on earth can claim. Whether you are an adrenaline junkie or a weekend wanderer, world-class adventure is always less than an hour away. ​Vertical Adventures: Scale legendary sandstone cliffs in what is widely considered the premier rock climbing hub of the Southeast.
